name: Yara Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and lead a small crew repairing timber roofs on building sites. I have a vocational trade certificate and can read an old rafter better than most, but the family builder pays below the usual rate. I like making a roof sound again; rain can cancel the day after we've travelled there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works variable shifts at a food warehouse, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. There is less than a month of expenses in our account and only a few similar builders nearby. I've never used AI, and I use a paper drawing and a probe to decide whether a beam is sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my roof crew a quicker invoice is fine, but it doesn't hold up a rotten beam. We still have to find sound timber and make the joint fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the repair crew and know old roofs well, yet the family builder pays below the usual rate. Rain cancels days, my partner's warehouse shifts vary, and we have less than a month saved against the mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll finish the market hall roof repairs and keep a written record of cancelled rain days. At home we'll stop the extra takeaway night for now and use that new spare money toward the next mortgage payment, rather than treating our tiny reserve as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even in the mild picture. The work may stay familiar. The next wet week on a roof could take more wages than office software saves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did weather cut your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month we lost two paid days when water reached the roof deck. I still went up afterward to mark which beam ends needed replacing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending would actually change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep the ordinary food shop and the children's school travel. The extra takeaway is the first expense to go because it is optional, not because AI forced it.

say: **Roof repairs** still need a worker to test timber and fit a sound joint.
A faster **invoice** will not stop weather cancellations.
think: My **lead skill** has not brought typical trade pay.
Under a month of **savings** leaves rainy weeks dangerous for the mortgage.
do: **Finish** market hall roof repairs and record cancelled rain days.
**Stop** the extra takeaway night to protect the next mortgage payment.
feel: **Anxious** about existing paid-day losses even if AI barely changes work.
S0.quote: The next wet week on a roof could take more wages than office software saves.
fieldNote: She has **high practical standing** but low pay and an under-month reserve, so the plateau does not secure her income.
Her **spending cut** names a discretionary takeaway; she protects food and school travel and does not relabel savings.

steps.text: Finish market hall roof repairs and record cancelled rain days
Stop extra takeaway night to protect next mortgage payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI will book timber and draw repair schedules before a robot climbs an old roof. A screen should not decide that a wet roof is safe because the calendar says Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the office packs more jobs into fewer days, my crew could lose paid time when repairs overrun. We have few nearby builders and a thin account, so even small changes in the rota matter to our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll photograph the next three rotten beam ends and write the actual repair time beside the office schedule. If the builder adopts AI booking, I'll ask for those measurements to be checked before the crew is moved, and keep working from the printed plan myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about more broken days and smaller pay packets, not about a robot arriving next week. I would rather show a real beam than argue about a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the scheduler about a soft beam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the scheduler a beam end is soft only after I probe it, then send the photograph and the repair time. I won't promise a same-day roof repair from a drawing made indoors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the builder's owner to change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the three repair times to the owner and ask for enough paid hours on the next roof. I have never used an AI tool and I do not plan to learn this booking system just to make the office's numbers look neat.

say: **AI booking** may change roof schedules before hands-on robots arrive.
A **wet roof** and rotten beam need field checks before time is promised.
think: Faster scheduling could shrink my **paid repair hours** when work overruns.
Few local builders and a **thin buffer** make smaller pay packets hard to absorb.
do: **Record** three beam repairs with photos and actual hours.
**Ask** owner to check AI bookings against paid roof repair times.
feel: **Anxious** about rota pressure and realistic paid-hour loss.
S1.quote: I won't promise a same-day roof repair from a drawing made indoors.
fieldNote: Her concern is **paid-hour loss** from compressed bookings; she supplies measured evidence without personally learning AI.
She remains **resistant to new technology**, preferring a printed plan and a direct discussion with the owner.

steps.text: Record three roof beam repairs with photographs and actual hours
Ask owner to check AI bookings against paid roof repair times

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 may plan the repair, then capable robots around 2031 may work on the roof itself. I would ask the owner which paid roof shifts might change before anyone signs a machine order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 48 when robots could replace hands-on repairs. My skill on old timber may still count, but with less than a month saved, lower pay and few other builders, a cut in my own shifts would hurt quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner this week for a written roof crew rota and any robot trial dates. If the builder cuts my paid shifts, I'll apply only to a posted local carpentry or repair vacancy with dependable hours and wages that cover our mortgage; until then I'll stay on the roof crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible cut, but I can still ask questions and keep working. I don't expect a dismissal notice this week, and I won't invent a course place that hasn't been offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner what the reserve can do. Our little reserve could cover a short gap in roof wages, not a whole season without work. We would check the mortgage and warehouse rota together before changing the children's routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another repair job viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look for a real notice with a wage and weekly hours, not a builder's casual promise. If the pay is lower than our mortgage needs, I cannot take the job just because it has a familiar title.

say: **2028 thinking AI** plans repairs before roof robots arrive around 2031.
The owner should name **paid roof shifts** before buying a machine.
think: At about **48**, fewer roof shifts could quickly threaten our mortgage.
My **old-timber skill** helps, but the tiny reserve and few local jobs limit choices.
do: **Ask** owner for written roof rota and robot trial dates this week.
**Apply** after paid-shift cuts only to posted local repair jobs covering mortgage.
**Stay** on current paid roof crew until a suitable offer exists.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage cut, still able to act.
S2.quote: Our little reserve could cover a short gap in roof wages, not a whole season without work.
fieldNote: She fears a **possible reduction** in her own roof shifts, not a certain major dismissal, and retains a concrete plan.
Her job move requires **an actual cut** plus a posted local vacancy, dependable hours and mortgage-covering wage; there is no invented course.

steps.text: Ask owner for written roof rota and robot trial dates
Apply after shift cut to posted local repair job with dependable mortgage-covering pay
Stay on paid roof crew until suitable offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 thinking AI could make the repair drawings and robots around 2034 could climb the roof. Five years gives our little firm time to say what a worker would still do and how many hours it would pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 51 I still expect to need a wage. I have good roof skills, but I cannot take unpaid months to learn a machine while the mortgage and two schoolchildren rely on our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the owner for a five-year site plan and a priced, paid training offer if machine maintenance becomes a real role. If there is a posted local building repair vacancy with dependable mortgage-covering pay and our firm announces shift cuts, I'll apply; otherwise I'll maintain the roof repair rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, though more warning lets me look at actual offers. I don't want to leave a working roof for a promise on a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make machine maintenance training possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for course fees covered and my normal pay for every training day before signing up. An invitation to watch a robot work is just information to me, not a new qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you test a repair vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the repair vacancy's weekly hours, travel cost and pay against our mortgage. If the numbers fail, I will keep looking while I still have the current job.

say: **2031 thinking AI** changes drawings before robots repair roofs around 2034.
A small builder should set out **paid roles and hours** before a machine trial.
think: At about **51**, I still need paid roof work for the mortgage.
Unpaid months of **machine training** are impossible with our thin reserve.
do: **Ask** owner for five-year roof crew plan and paid training terms.
**Apply** after shift cuts only to posted local repair vacancy with dependable mortgage-covering pay.
**Maintain** paid roof repair rota while no suitable offer exists.
feel: **Anxious** about possible hour cuts, with time to check offers.
S3.quote: An invitation to watch a robot work is just information to me, not a new qualification.
fieldNote: She asks about **funded training terms** but makes no enrolment decision, so retraining is not an action.
A new role must be **posted, local and mortgage-covering** with dependable hours, and follows an announced shift cut.

steps.text: Ask owner for roof crew plan and funded paid-time training terms
Apply after cuts to posted local repair job with dependable mortgage-covering pay
Maintain paid roof repair rota while no suitable offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 may draw repairs and capable robots around 2039 may climb the roof. Ten years would let us repair a lot of real buildings before a machine becomes the carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 56 at the robot date, with the children older but a mortgage balance I cannot guess today. The present thin savings and weather gaps still make me anxious even if the technology arrives slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my roof safety certificate current and record every lost weather shift this year. My partner and I will try to put fifteen from each full paid week into a new reserve if the warehouse and site hours hold; if they do not, we will not claim the existing account grew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's income, with a longer chance to prepare for machines. I can count full paid weeks, but I can't promise how many the weather gives us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you track a new reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write the deposit beside each full paid week in the household notebook. If my roof crew has no full paid weeks, I cannot add to savings, and the mortgage comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What counts as a full paid week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A full week means the site actually pays all scheduled hours, not just that I was willing to work them. We would check the warehouse rota as well before moving money into the reserve.

say: **2036 thinking AI** changes drawings before roof robots arrive around 2039.
A decade gives workers time to maintain **site safety skills** and track wages.
think: At about **56**, the mortgage may still need my roof wage.
Today's **weather gaps** and tiny reserve keep us exposed even with a long runway.
do: **Keep** roof safety certificate current and record lost weather shifts.
**Deposit** fifteen from each full paid week if site and warehouse hours hold.
feel: **Anxious** about current wage gaps despite more time before robots.
S4.quote: If my roof crew has no full paid weeks, I cannot add to savings, and the mortgage comes first.
fieldNote: Her **new saving** requires a full paid site week and stable warehouse hours; the existing under-month account is not recounted.
The long scenario leaves **current weather-driven wage risk** intact, so anxiety follows her household facts rather than a robot forecast.

steps.text: Keep roof safety certificate current and record weather-shift losses
Deposit fifteen from full paid week if site and warehouse hours hold

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because roof robots around 2031 could cut paid repair shifts while we already have almost no buffer. A written crew rota and a real, local repair vacancy with dependable mortgage-covering pay would help if hours fall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the robot will get paid when rain stops the roof work, because our crew does not. The mortgage letter arrives on a dry day and a wet day alike. I want paid hours before any talk about a new machine.

headlineQuote: The mortgage letter arrives on a dry day and a wet day alike.
portrait: **Yara**, 43, leads timber roof repairs with a vocational certificate and strong site skill despite lower trade pay.
Her warehouse-worker partner and two schoolchildren share a **mortgage** with her; savings cover less than one month.
She has **never used AI**, prefers paper drawings and has only a few similar local building jobs.
Existing weather gaps make her **anxious** even in the plateau; robot scenarios add possible paid-hour cuts and conditional job searches.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring roof robots around 2031 while she already has almost no wage buffer.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew rota** and posted local repair job with dependable mortgage-covering pay would help if shifts fall.
